entities.summary:
Liu Ling (c. 221–300 CE) was a prominent Chinese poet and scholar of the Western Jin dynasty, celebrated as one of the 'Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove' (Zhulin Qixian). Born into a period of profound political instability and intellectual ferment following the collapse of the Han dynasty, Liu Ling embraced Neo-Daoist (Xuanxue) philosophy, advocating for a life of natural spontaneity and detachment from rigid Confucian social conventions. His significance lies in embodying the counter-cultural intellectualism of his era, using poetry and eccentric behavior to critique the prevailing political and social order, thereby influencing the trajectory of Chinese literary and philosophical thought.

His primary surviving work, the 'Ode to Wine' (Jiu de song), is a masterful exposition of his hedonistic yet philosophically grounded approach to life. In this poem, Liu Ling extols the virtues of intoxication as a means of achieving spiritual liberation and escaping worldly anxieties, famously declaring, 'When I am drunk, I am not concerned with the affairs of the world.' He was known for his unconventional lifestyle, including riding naked in a deer cart and having a servant follow him with a shovel, ready to bury him wherever he might fall dead. These acts were not mere eccentricity but deliberate, performative rejections of societal norms, expressing a profound disillusionment with the officialdom and moral hypocrisy of his time.
